extendedContent.title: Origins & Mythology
extendedContent.content: Coatlicue's origins are deeply rooted in the Aztec understanding of the earth as a living, breathing entity. She is often associated with the primordial goddess Tlaltecuhtli, who was dismembered to create the world. The myth of Coatlicue's impregnation by a ball of feathers is central to her story. While sweeping the temple, a ball of feathers fell on her, and she became pregnant with Huitzilopochtli. Her other children, Coyolxauhqui and the Centzon Huitznahua (the southern stars), were angered by this and plotted to kill her. However, Huitzilopochtli sprang from her womb, fully armed, and defeated them, establishing his dominance and fulfilling his destiny as the sun god. This myth explains the origin of the sun and moon and reinforces the importance of sacrifice in maintaining cosmic order.

extendedContent.title: Role & Significance
extendedContent.content: Coatlicue played a vital role in Aztec religion and cosmology. As the earth goddess, she was responsible for the fertility of the land and the abundance of crops. She was also seen as the mother of all living things, both human and divine. Her complex and often terrifying imagery served as a reminder of the power and unpredictability of nature. She was honored in various rituals and ceremonies, often involving offerings of food and precious objects. Her temple, located in the heart of Tenochtitlan, was a significant center of worship. Coatlicue's significance extends beyond her role as a deity; she embodies the cyclical nature of existence, reminding the Aztecs of the constant interplay between life and death, creation and destruction.

extendedContent.title: Symbolism & Interpretation
extendedContent.content: Coatlicue's symbolism is rich and multifaceted. Her serpent skirt represents the earth's fertility and the interconnectedness of all things. The serpents themselves are symbols of power, transformation, and the cyclical nature of time. The necklace of human hands and hearts symbolizes the sacrifices necessary to sustain life and maintain cosmic balance. Her severed head, sometimes replaced by serpents, represents the flow of blood and the life force that nourishes the earth. Overall, Coatlicue embodies the duality of the earth: its capacity for both nurturing and consuming, creation and destruction. She is a powerful symbol of the interconnectedness of all things and the constant cycle of life, death, and rebirth. Her fearsome appearance served as a reminder of the power and unpredictability of nature, urging the Aztecs to respect and appease the gods through ritual and sacrifice.

extendedContent.title: Legacy & Influence
extendedContent.content: Coatlicue's legacy continues to resonate in modern Mexican culture and art. Her iconic image has been reinterpreted by numerous artists and writers, often as a symbol of indigenous identity and resistance. The discovery of the monumental Coatlicue statue in Mexico City in the 18th century sparked renewed interest in Aztec art and mythology. Today, Coatlicue remains a powerful symbol of the earth's power and the enduring strength of indigenous traditions. Her complex and multifaceted nature continues to inspire artists, scholars, and spiritual seekers alike. She serves as a reminder of the interconnectedness of all things and the importance of honoring the earth and its cycles.

subtitle: Serpent Skirt: Mother of Gods and Earth
shortDescription: Coatlicue, "Serpent Skirt", is the Aztec earth goddess and mother of the gods, most famously the mother of Huitzilopochtli, the god of war.
name: Coatlicue

description: Coatlicue, meaning "Serpent Skirt" or "She of the Serpent Skirt," is a prominent and complex figure in Aztec mythology. She is revered as the earth goddess, the mother of gods, and a symbol of both creation and destruction. Coatlicue's imagery is striking and often fearsome, reflecting her dual nature. She is typically depicted wearing a skirt of intertwined serpents, a necklace of human hands and hearts, and her severed head is sometimes replaced by two serpents, symbolizing the flow of blood and life force. According to legend, Coatlicue was impregnated by a ball of feathers and miraculously gave birth to Huitzilopochtli, the god of war, who sprang forth fully armed to defeat his siblings, who plotted to kill her. This myth highlights Coatlicue's role as a powerful maternal figure and the source of cosmic conflict. She is also associated with the cyclical nature of life, death, and rebirth, embodying the earth's capacity for both nurturing and consuming.
